lit: bright and clear, upright and great: done in full daylight with nothing to hide

use.how: Mostly adverbial (光明正大地提出来) or a predicate (做事光明正大). Said of how something is done: in the open, by the rules, with nothing hidden.

near.diff: 光明磊落 praises a person's open, honest character; 光明正大 usually describes doing a particular thing openly rather than in secret.

cue: People hint that you won the contract through a backroom deal. You insist everything was done in the open and anyone may check.

ctx.s: 我们是按规矩办事，{光明正大}，不怕别人查。
ctx.en: We did it by the rules, all in the open; we're not afraid of anyone checking.

ctx.s: 你想请假就{光明正大}地说，别装病。
ctx.en: If you want a day off, just say so openly; don't pretend to be ill.

ctx.s: 有意见可以在会上{光明正大}地提出来，何必在背后议论？
ctx.en: If you disagree, raise it openly in the meeting. Why gossip behind people's backs?

ctx.s: “这笔钱是我凭本事赚来的，来得{光明正大}！”
ctx.en: "I earned this money by my own ability; I came by it fair and square!"

ctx.s: 他喜欢她，就{光明正大}地追求，从不偷偷摸摸。
ctx.en: He liked her, so he courted her openly, never sneaking around.

ctx.s: 这次招标全程公开，评选过程{光明正大}，落选的公司也没话说。
ctx.en: The tender was public from start to finish and the selection was above board, so even the losing firms had nothing to say.

bad.s: 这个房间窗户很大，非常{光明正大}。
bad.en: (meant: the room is very bright)
bad.why: It is about honest, open conduct, not about light. A bright room is míngliàng.

bad.s: 他拿了冠军，大家都觉得非常{光明正大}。
bad.en: (meant: everyone thought it was glorious)
bad.why: It does not mean glorious or honourable (that is guāngróng); it only says something was done openly and fairly.

lit: like ghosts and haunting spirits, creeping about where no one should see

use.how: Adverbial (鬼鬼祟祟地看), predicate (他鬼鬼祟祟的) or attributive (鬼鬼祟祟的人). Describes someone's shifty, suspicious manner.

near.diff: 偷偷摸摸 stresses doing something secretly; 鬼鬼祟祟 stresses that the person looks shifty and suspicious while doing it.
光明正大 is its opposite: acting openly with nothing to hide.

cue: A stranger keeps peering over your neighbour's fence, ducking whenever someone looks his way. How does he look?

ctx.s: 门口有个人{鬼鬼祟祟}的，一直往院子里看。
ctx.en: There's someone acting suspiciously at the gate, staring into the yard the whole time.

ctx.s: 你{鬼鬼祟祟}地躲在门后干什么？
ctx.en: What are you doing skulking behind the door?

ctx.s: 保安发现一个男人在停车场{鬼鬼祟祟}地拉车门，就上前询问。
ctx.en: The guard saw a man furtively trying car doors in the car park and went over to question him.

ctx.s: “他俩在角落里{鬼鬼祟祟}地说什么呢？”“可能在给你准备惊喜吧。”
ctx.en: "What are those two whispering about so shiftily in the corner?" "Maybe they're planning a surprise for you."

ctx.s: 雨夜里，一个{鬼鬼祟祟}的身影溜进了旅馆的后门。
ctx.en: On a rainy night, a furtive figure slipped in through the hotel's back door.

ctx.s: 有话就当面说，别总是{鬼鬼祟祟}的，让人心里不舒服。
ctx.en: If you've got something to say, say it to my face. Always sneaking around makes people uneasy.

bad.s: 侦探{鬼鬼祟祟}地破了案，大家都很佩服他。
bad.en: (meant: the detective solved the case discreetly and cleverly)
bad.why: It is a criticism of shifty, suspicious behaviour and cannot be used as praise for discretion.

bad.s: 这座老房子很{鬼鬼祟祟}，晚上没人敢进去。
bad.en: (meant: the old house is spooky)
bad.why: Despite the ghost in it, it describes how a person behaves, not an eerie or haunted place.

use.how: Predicate or attributive describing a child or young person (这孩子聪明伶俐；聪明伶俐的小姑娘). Not used of grown adults' learning, nor as an adverb.

cue: Your friend's five-year-old learns a card game in one go and chats politely with every guest. How do you compliment the child?

ctx.s: 这孩子{聪明伶俐}，一教就会。
ctx.en: This child is so bright: show him once and he's got it.

ctx.s: 邻居家的小女儿{聪明伶俐}，见了谁都甜甜地打招呼。
ctx.en: The neighbours' little daughter is bright and quick, and greets everyone sweetly.

ctx.s: “你家儿子真是{聪明伶俐}啊！”“哪里哪里，就是嘴快。”
ctx.en: "Your son is so bright!" "Oh, not really, he's just a chatterbox."

ctx.s: 奶奶逢人就夸她那个{聪明伶俐}的小孙子。
ctx.en: Grandma boasts to everyone she meets about her clever little grandson.

ctx.s: 店里新来的小学徒{聪明伶俐}，师傅很喜欢他。
ctx.en: The young new apprentice at the shop is sharp and quick, and the master is very fond of him.

ctx.s: 故事里的小狐狸{聪明伶俐}，几次都骗过了猎人。
ctx.en: The little fox in the story is clever and quick-witted, and fools the hunter again and again.

bad.s: 这位老教授{聪明伶俐}，学问很深。
bad.en: (meant: the old professor is brilliant and learned)
bad.why: It praises a child's or young person's quickness and charm; said of an elderly scholar it sounds patronising.

bad.s: 他{聪明伶俐}地解决了这个技术问题。
bad.en: (meant: he solved the technical problem cleverly)
bad.why: It describes what a person is like, not how an action is done, so it is not used as an adverb before a verb.

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (笨手笨脚地包饺子). Mild criticism of physical clumsiness, often said of oneself or of a beginner.

near.diff: 手忙脚乱 is being flustered because there is too much to do at once; 笨手笨脚 is lacking skill or coordination even when there is no rush.

cue: Helping in a friend's kitchen, you drop an egg, knock over the salt and nick your finger peeling a potato. You apologise for being what?

ctx.s: 我{笨手笨脚}的，又把杯子打碎了。
ctx.en: I'm so clumsy, I've broken another cup.

ctx.s: 第一次包饺子，他{笨手笨脚}地捏了半天也没捏好。
ctx.en: Making dumplings for the first time, he fumbled with them for ages and still couldn't seal them.

ctx.s: “让我来吧，你{笨手笨脚}的，别把孩子弄醒了。”
ctx.en: "Let me do it; you're all thumbs, you'll wake the baby."

ctx.s: 新来的服务员有点{笨手笨脚}，客人不多也老是打翻杯子。
ctx.en: The new waiter is a bit clumsy: even when there are few customers he keeps knocking over glasses.

ctx.s: 别看他平时{笨手笨脚}，修起自行车来可灵巧了。
ctx.en: He may seem clumsy most of the time, but he's really deft when it comes to fixing bikes.

ctx.s: 小熊{笨手笨脚}地爬上树，想去够蜂蜜。
ctx.en: The little bear clambered clumsily up the tree, trying to reach the honey.

bad.s: 他{笨手笨脚}，数学总是考不及格。
bad.en: (meant: he's slow-witted and always fails maths)
bad.why: It is about clumsy hands and movements, not about intelligence or being a slow learner.

bad.s: 这把椅子太{笨手笨脚}了，搬起来很费劲。
bad.en: (meant: the chair is bulky and hard to move)
bad.why: Only people and animals have clumsy hands and feet; a bulky, heavy object is bènzhòng.

story.text: When King Wu of Zhou fell gravely ill, his brother the Duke of Zhou prayed to their ancestors and offered to die in the king's place. He argued that he himself was gifted with many talents and many arts and could serve the spirits well, while the king was less suited to it but was needed to rule the people.

use.how: Predicate or attributive about a person (她多才多艺；多才多艺的人). Praises skill across several fields such as music, art, sport or crafts.

near.diff: 才华横溢 is brimming over with talent, often in one field such as writing; 多才多艺 stresses the range of different skills.

cue: Your new colleague plays the guitar at the party, shows you her oil paintings and turns out to have coached the school football team.

ctx.s: 她{多才多艺}，会弹钢琴，还会画画。
ctx.en: She's very versatile: she plays the piano and paints as well.

ctx.s: 新来的同事{多才多艺}，年会上又唱又跳。
ctx.en: Our new colleague is multi-talented: at the annual party he sang and danced.

ctx.s: “你还会做木工？真是{多才多艺}！”
ctx.en: "You do woodwork too? You really can do everything!"

ctx.s: 学校希望把学生培养成{多才多艺}的人，而不只是会考试。
ctx.en: The school wants to raise all-round, versatile students, not just good exam-takers.

ctx.s: 这位作家{多才多艺}，写小说之余还拍过两部电影。
ctx.en: This writer is remarkably versatile; besides novels, she has also made two films.

ctx.s: 别看他只是个司机，其实{多才多艺}，书法写得特别好。
ctx.en: He may only be a driver, but he's actually very gifted in many ways; his calligraphy is superb.

bad.s: 他{多才多艺}，一辈子只研究物理一门学问。
bad.en: (meant: he was extremely talented, devoting his life to physics)
bad.why: It means talented in many different areas, so it contradicts devotion to a single field.

bad.s: 这家餐厅{多才多艺}，川菜粤菜都有。
bad.en: (meant: the restaurant has a varied menu)
bad.why: It praises a person's talents, not the range of dishes or goods a business offers.

mean: leaving early and coming home late
lit: go out early, come back late

use.how: Predicate (他每天早出晚归). Describes someone's daily pattern of being away from home all day, for work, study or travel.

near.diff: 起早贪黑 stresses hard toil from dawn into the night; 早出晚归 only says the person leaves early and gets home late.

cue: Your neighbour is gone before you wake and back after you're asleep; in a month you've hardly seen him.

ctx.s: 爸爸上班的地方很远，每天{早出晚归}，我很少能跟他一起吃饭。
ctx.en: Dad works a long way off and leaves early and comes home late every day, so I rarely get to eat with him.

ctx.s: 他最近{早出晚归}的，邻居快一个月没见到他了。
ctx.en: He's been out from early till late lately; the neighbours haven't seen him for almost a month.

ctx.s: 旅游那几天我们{早出晚归}，把城里的景点全逛遍了。
ctx.en: On that trip we went out early and came back late every day, and saw every sight in the city.

ctx.s: “你这阵子怎么{早出晚归}？”“公司搬到郊区了，路上要两个小时。”
ctx.en: "Why are you leaving so early and getting back so late these days?" "The office moved to the suburbs; it's a two-hour commute."

ctx.s: 为了不吵醒室友，他{早出晚归}时总是轻手轻脚的。
ctx.en: So as not to wake his roommate, he always moves quietly when he goes out early and comes back late.

ctx.s: 搬到新城市后，她{早出晚归}，三个月后才发现楼下有家面馆。
ctx.en: After moving to the new city she was out from morning till night, and only found the noodle shop downstairs three months later.

bad.s: 我习惯{早出晚归}，每天晚上九点就睡觉。
bad.en: (meant: I keep early hours and go to bed at nine)
bad.why: It means being out of the house from early till late, not going to bed early (that is zǎo shuì zǎo qǐ).

bad.s: 这家超市{早出晚归}，买东西很方便。
bad.en: (meant: the supermarket opens early and closes late)
bad.why: It describes a person leaving home and coming back, not a shop's long opening hours.

mean: working long hours from dawn till dark
lit: rise early and be greedy for the dark, working on after nightfall

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (起早贪黑地干活). Said, often with sympathy or respect, of people who toil long hours to make a living or reach a goal.

near.diff: 早出晚归 only describes leaving early and returning late; 起早贪黑 stresses the hard work filling those hours.
废寝忘食 is being so absorbed that one forgets meals and sleep; 起早贪黑 is long hours of hard labour, often out of necessity.

cue: Your parents ran a small noodle stall, up before dawn to make dough and closing after dark, to pay for your schooling.

ctx.s: 他们夫妻俩{起早贪黑}地开小饭馆，供两个孩子上大学。
ctx.en: The couple worked dawn to dusk running a little restaurant to put their two children through university.

ctx.s: 为了多挣点钱，她{起早贪黑}，白天送快递，晚上去饭馆洗碗。
ctx.en: To earn a bit more, she works from dawn till dark: delivering parcels by day and washing dishes in a restaurant at night.

ctx.s: “我{起早贪黑}地干，一个月才挣这么点儿？”
ctx.en: "I slave away from morning to night, and this is all I earn in a month?"

ctx.s: 父母{起早贪黑}把我们养大，现在该我们照顾他们了。
ctx.en: Our parents worked themselves to the bone raising us; now it's our turn to look after them.

ctx.s: 菜市场的摊主大多{起早贪黑}，凌晨就去批发市场进货。
ctx.en: Most market stallholders work long hours, going to the wholesale market before dawn to buy stock.

ctx.s: 别光知道{起早贪黑}地加班，身体累垮了可不值得。
ctx.en: Don't just work overtime from dawn to dark; it isn't worth wrecking your health.

bad.s: 我们这次度假{起早贪黑}，玩得特别开心。
bad.en: (meant: on holiday we were out sightseeing from morning to night)
bad.why: It means toiling at hard work, so it clashes with a fun holiday; for a busy sightseeing day use zǎo chū wǎn guī.

bad.s: 我每天{起早贪黑}，所以精神特别好。
bad.en: (meant: I keep early hours, so I feel great)
bad.why: It means working from dawn until after dark, which is exhausting, not a healthy early-to-bed routine.

lit: push it away three times, block it four times

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (别推三阻四；他推三阻四地不肯去). Criticises someone who keeps finding pretexts to dodge a request or duty.

cue: You ask your flatmate to help move a sofa. First he has a call, then a sore back, then he suddenly has to go out.

ctx.s: 让他帮个小忙，他却{推三阻四}的。
ctx.en: I asked him for a small favour and he kept making excuses.

ctx.s: 你要是不想去就直说，别{推三阻四}。
ctx.en: If you don't want to go, just say so; stop making excuses.

ctx.s: 每次轮到他打扫卫生，他总是{推三阻四}，不是头疼就是有事。
ctx.en: Whenever it's his turn to clean, he finds one excuse after another: a headache, or something else to do.

ctx.s: “借你的车用一下，你{推三阻四}干什么？又不是不还。”
ctx.en: "I only want to borrow your car. Why all the excuses? I'll bring it back."

ctx.s: 房东答应修热水器，可一个多月了还在{推三阻四}。
ctx.en: The landlord promised to fix the water heater, but over a month later he's still stalling with excuses.

ctx.s: 记者想采访负责人，对方{推三阻四}，始终不肯露面。
ctx.en: The reporter wanted to interview the person in charge, but they kept putting him off and never appeared.

bad.s: 他出于礼貌{推三阻四}，最后才收下了礼物。
bad.en: (meant: out of politeness he declined the gift several times before accepting)
bad.why: It criticises dodging a duty with excuses; politely refusing a gift several times is zàisān tuīcí.

bad.s: 门卡住了，他{推三阻四}才把门推开。
bad.en: (meant: he pushed the stuck door several times before it opened)
bad.why: The pushing here is figurative, pushing a task away; it is never about physically pushing something.

use.how: Predicate or attributive (他身强力壮；身强力壮的小伙子). Describes a person's physical strength, usually a young or middle-aged adult.

near.diff: 年富力强 is being in the prime of life with energy and experience, said of careers; 身强力壮 is only about bodily strength.

cue: The removal men cancelled. You need someone who can carry a fridge up four flights of stairs, and your burly cousin comes to mind.

ctx.s: 他{身强力壮}，一个人就把冰箱搬上了楼。
ctx.en: He's big and strong: he carried the fridge upstairs on his own.

ctx.s: 你们几个{身强力壮}的小伙子，过来帮忙抬一下桌子。
ctx.en: You strong young lads, come and help lift this table.

ctx.s: 爷爷年轻时{身强力壮}，一口气能挑两担水。
ctx.en: When Grandpa was young he was so strong he could carry two loads of water on a pole without a rest.

ctx.s: “你{身强力壮}的，怎么连这点活儿都嫌累？”
ctx.en: "A strong fellow like you, and this little job is too tiring?"

ctx.s: 救援队挑了几名{身强力壮}的队员进山搜救。
ctx.en: The rescue team picked several of its strongest members to search the mountains.

ctx.s: 就算{身强力壮}，经常熬夜身体也会出问题。
ctx.en: Even if you're strong and fit, staying up late all the time will damage your health.

bad.s: 她有{身强力壮}的意志，从来不放弃。
bad.en: (meant: she has a strong will and never gives up)
bad.why: It is only about the physical strength of the body; a strong will is yìzhì jiānqiáng.

bad.s: 这座桥修得{身强力壮}，再大的车也能过。
bad.en: (meant: the bridge is sturdy)
bad.why: It describes people's bodies, not objects; a sturdy bridge is jiāngù or jiēshi.

lit: breath heaving, puffing and blowing (xū xū imitates the sound of panting)

use.how: Adverbial (气喘吁吁地跑来) or predicate, often after 累得 (累得气喘吁吁). Describes heavy breathing after running, climbing or carrying.

near.diff: 筋疲力尽 is being utterly exhausted in general; 气喘吁吁 is the visible, audible panting right after exertion.

cue: The lift is broken. Your friend arrives at your sixth-floor flat, chest heaving, unable to say hello for a moment.

ctx.s: 他一路跑上五楼，到了门口还在{气喘吁吁}。
ctx.en: He ran all the way up to the fifth floor and was still panting at the door.

ctx.s: 快递员{气喘吁吁}地把箱子搬到了门口。
ctx.en: Puffing and panting, the courier carried the box to the door.

ctx.s: “你怎么{气喘吁吁}的？后面有人追你吗？”
ctx.en: "Why are you so out of breath? Is someone chasing you?"

ctx.s: 才爬了几层台阶，我就{气喘吁吁}，看来真该锻炼了。
ctx.en: I'd only climbed a few flights of steps and I was already puffing; I really need to get some exercise.

ctx.s: 他{气喘吁吁}地赶到车站，火车刚刚开走。
ctx.en: He reached the station, panting, just as the train pulled out.

ctx.s: 小女孩{气喘吁吁}地跑进教室，大声说：“老师，下雪了！”
ctx.en: The little girl ran into the classroom out of breath and cried, "Teacher, it's snowing!"

bad.s: 他听了这话{气喘吁吁}，大骂起来。
bad.en: (meant: hearing that, he was furious and started shouting)
bad.why: The qì here is breath, not anger; it describes panting after exertion, not fury.

bad.s: 想了一整天方案，我心里{气喘吁吁}的。
bad.en: (meant: after a day of planning I'm mentally drained)
bad.why: It describes physical panting only and cannot be used for mental tiredness.
